title: The sharp upper edge of the normalised distance Laplacian
shortTitle: How close the distance Laplacian can get to two
oneLine: The largest eigenvalue over n-vertex graphs is 2 − 4/√(3n) + o(1/√n), with the shape of every near-maximiser
abstract: Reinhart's normalised distance Laplacian turns the distance matrix of a connected graph into a random walk that prefers distant vertices; its largest eigenvalue lies below 2, and the deficit measures how far the walk is from swinging perfectly back and forth. Johnston and Tait proved that the maximum over graphs with n vertices tends to 2, placed the smallest deficit between about 1/n and 2√2/√n, proved the order 1/√n under extra eigenvector conditions and asked for the true order. This candidate proves that the smallest deficit is 4/√(3n) to first order, with no extra conditions, and that every near-extremal graph looks at large scale like a path of length about √(3n) with half of the vertices in a nearly complete cluster at each end; the extremal eigenvector falls linearly along the path. The same method gives sharp constants for distance powers d^α, for trees (4√(2/3) at α = 1) and for graphs excluding a fixed subgraph with a cycle. Exhaustive computations reproduce Reinhart's extremal graphs up to 9 vertices and find that two stars joined by a path are optimal among all trees with 6 to 20 vertices, stated as a conjecture. Limits: first order only, so Reinhart's exact conjecture stays open; the second-order term is observed numerically only. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

evidence: A 16-page paper with a plain introduction (the question, what was known, what is new, what is not settled, the idea of the proof and a roadmap) and written proofs of every theorem and corollary. Five Python programs accompany it: verify.py checks exact characteristic polynomials, exact trial quotients of both constructions up to n = 10^8, full spectra for several distance powers and weights, and the bounded-weight inequality; finite_search.py runs exhaustive searches over all connected graphs with up to 9 vertices and all trees with up to 20 vertices (nauty) and the large-order family optima; two further scripts recompute the trial quotients and the bounded-weight inequality by separate code; figure.py draws Figure 1. A clean replay in Python's optimised mode reproduced the three quick outputs byte for byte and the exhaustive search under the declared comparison policy; changing one exact check makes verify.py fail; Linux CI reruns the quick scripts. The computations accompany the written proofs; they do not replace them.

keyResults: Theorem 1 (proof): lim √n (2 − M_n) = 4/√3 ≈ 2.31, where M_n is the largest spectral radius of the normalised distance Laplacian over connected graphs with n vertices; this answers Johnston and Tait's question on the order of the gap.

Theorem 1(a)–(c) (proof): every near-extremal sequence has diameter (√3 + o(1))√n, two disjoint sets of (1/2 + o(1))n vertices with edge density tending to one, and measured Gromov–Hausdorff limit [0,1] with half of the mass at each end.
Theorem 2 (proof): for distance weights d^α with fixed α > 0, sharp constants K_{α,b} for all graphs, K_{κ+1}-free graphs and trees; at α = 1 the tree constant is 4√(2/3) ≈ 3.27.

Corollaries 8, 9, 11 and Theorem 10 (proof): graphs excluding a fixed subgraph with a cycle, the limiting extremal eigenvector and the rest of the spectrum, regularly varying weights and bounded weights.

Computation (Section 11): clique–path–clique graphs attain the minimum deficit among all connected graphs with 4 to 9 vertices; two stars joined by a path attain it among all trees with 6 to 20 vertices (Conjecture 12 for every n).

Limits and credit: first order only, so Reinhart's exact conjecture stays open; the second-order coefficient (about 4.26 at a million vertices) is numerical. The question, barbell construction and conditional order are due to Johnston and Tait; the matrix, conjecture and small table to Reinhart; the row-overlap inequality is the classical Doeblin–Dobrushin bound.
